title: With all his might (2 Samuel 6:14–16)
hook: the king dances before the ark; Michal despises it

segments.voice: Yesterday, David's lament for Saul and Jonathan. Your line was how are the mighty fallen. Did you find one true thing to grieve in someone hard? Today, the same man, and his whole body full of joy. Day seven hundred forty-four.

Shouting. The blast of the shofar. A crowd pressing up the road into Jerusalem, and in the middle of it, the ark of the covenant, carried up into the city. David is king now. He could ride beside it in robes, nodding to the crowd. Instead, he's out in front of it, in the dust of the road, and he's dancing. Not a polite sway. The kind of dancing that makes people stare. And up above the street, at a window, someone is watching him do it. The same woman who once lowered him through a window to save his life.
screen: `SHOUTING AND THE SHOFAR.` → `THE ARK COMES TO JERUSALEM.` → `A FACE AT THE WINDOW.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse: "And David danced before the LORD with all his might; and David was girded with a linen ephod." With all his might. The Hebrew is b'chol oz, with all strength. Nothing held back for his dignity. And notice what he's wearing. Not the king's robes. A linen ephod, a simple garment, the kind the text gives to priests and to the boy Samuel serving at the shrine. Some translators render his dancing as whirling. The next verses add leaping. A king spinning and jumping in the street. Then the camera moves to the window. Michal, the daughter of Saul, looks out, sees King David leaping and dancing before the Lord, and the text says she despised him in her heart. Notice how she's named. Not David's wife. The daughter of Saul, as if the old house is looking down at the new one. When David comes home, she meets him with sarcasm: how the king of Israel honored himself today, uncovering himself in front of the servants' maids. And David answers that it was before the Lord that he danced, and he'll be humbler still. Some readers hold this scene up as a picture of joy in God that doesn't stop to ask how it looks. Others make room for Michal's side: the woman at the first window gave everything for David, and at the second window she's only watching. Between those two windows, the book has told us, Saul gave her to another man, and David later had her taken back, while that husband walked behind her, weeping. It shows us a king who forgot himself, and a woman who couldn't.
screen: `B'CHOL OZ: WITH ALL STRENGTH.` · `A LINEN EPHOD, NOT ROBES.` · `MICHAL DESPISES HIM.` · then, large: `WITH ALL HIS MIGHT.` · then: `BEFORE THE LORD I DANCED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: dance without caring who's watching. If you're somewhere private, stand up. If you're not, or you can't stand, you can do this sitting: shoulders, hands, head, feet. Put on a song in your head, or a real one. Something that makes you glad. Then move to it, with all your might, for the length of the bell. Not well. Not for anyone. If a voice in your head says you look ridiculous, keep going anyway. If you pray, you can let the movement be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
With all his might. A king in a linen garment, dancing in the road before the ark, holding nothing back. Today's word.
Your line: with all his might. Today, do one glad thing full out, without checking who's looking. Day seven hundred forty-four.

howItsDone: Jews read David's dance before the ark in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets, and dancing with joy in worship carries on in Jewish life, as when people dance with the Torah scrolls on Simchat Torah.

what it means: David lays down his dignity before God, and Michal, watching from a window, despises him for it.
what a scholar hears: here she is called the daughter of Saul, not David's wife, as the old house looks down on the new.

notes: Verify JPS 1917 wording of 2 Samuel 6:14 (certain in the KJV).
'Some translators render his dancing as whirling' refers to the Hebrew mekharker; confirm.
Linen ephod on the boy Samuel is 1 Samuel 2:18; 'the kind the text gives to priests' also leans on 1 Samuel 22:18. Confirm.
Descriptions of the ark's contents were cut under the claims rule.
'Daughter of Saul ... the old house looking down on the new one' is a reading; confirm it is fair.
Michal's words and David's reply (6:20–22) are paraphrased; 6:23 is left out.
Simchat Torah dancing in howItsDone; confirm phrasing.
Editor: 'the girl at the first window' changed to 'the woman' (Michal was already David's wife in 1 Samuel 19), and the practice no longer tells the listener what voice they hear.

Audit: replaced 'the text doesn't tell us everything that happened between those two windows' with what the text does tell: Michal given to Palti (1 Samuel 25:44) and taken back by David's demand while her husband followed weeping (2 Samuel 3:14–16). This gives Michal's side its basis instead of leaving it vague.
